prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "CME GROUP INC." (ticker CME), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "CME", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: CME Group Inc.
markets: Interest rate futures and options (SOFR, U.S. Treasury)
Equity index futures and options (E-mini S&P 500, Nasdaq-100)
Energy futures and options (WTI crude, Henry Hub natural gas)
Agricultural futures and options (corn, soybeans, wheat, livestock)
Foreign exchange futures and spot FX (EBS)
Cash U.S. Treasury and repo trading (BrokerTec)
Market data and benchmarks (CME Term SOFR)
Clearing, including planned U.S. Treasury clearing
Crypto futures and retail prediction markets

mission.plain: CME Group describes itself as the world's leading derivatives marketplace, 'where the world comes to manage risk'.

about.plain: CME Group runs giant marketplaces where banks, farmers, airlines, investors and traders make deals today about prices in the future, for things like interest rates, stock indexes, oil, corn and gold. This lets people protect themselves if prices move the wrong way. CME charges a small fee on every contract and also guarantees the deals through its clearing house so no one is left unpaid. It also sells the price data from its markets.
about.customers: Banks, hedge funds, asset managers, trading firms, energy and farm businesses, and a growing number of individual traders through brokers.
about.everyday: The price of gasoline, the interest rate on your mortgage and the price of bread are all influenced by contracts traded on CME's markets.

money.part: Futures and options trading and clearing fees
money.plain: a fee for every contract traded and cleared on CME, CBOT, NYMEX and COMEX
selling real-time and historical price data and benchmark licences

money.part: Cash Treasury and FX trading (BrokerTec, EBS)
money.plain: electronic trading of U.S. government bonds, repo and currencies
clearing cash Treasury and repo trades ahead of SEC mandates (approved December 2025)
bitcoin, ether and other crypto futures and options
event contracts for everyday people through the FanDuel Predicts app launched December 2025

result.summary: CME has a wide moat: it owns the benchmark contracts in interest rates, equity indexes, oil, grains and gold, and because buyers and sellers want to trade where everyone else is, liquidity attracts more liquidity. Its vertically integrated clearing house adds margin offsets (about $72 billion a day of savings in 2025) that make switching costly, giving it operating margins near 65% and record revenue in 2025.

pricingPower.evidence: CME raises fees regularly without losing volume: it set up to 3.5% increases for 2027 market data, DataMine and licence fees and new CME Term SOFR licence fees, while market data revenue grew 13% in 2025 and 20% in Q3 2026; 2025 ADV hit a record 28.1 million contracts and Q3 2026 ADV rose 16.3% even as the average rate per contract slipped to $0.679 from $0.702 on mix.

moats.evidence: Brand Finance named CME the most valuable exchange brand for the 11th year in a row (USD 2.4 billion), and it owns benchmark contracts such as E-mini S&P 500, WTI crude, SOFR and Treasury futures plus CME Term SOFR, the only SOFR term rate endorsed by the ARRC.

Its clearing house nets margin across products, saving clients about $72 billion a day in 2025 and $100 billion a day in Q3 2026; open interest cannot be moved to a rival exchange, so leaving means losing offsets.

Liquidity begets liquidity: record 2025 ADV of 28.1 million contracts with 93% on CME Globex makes its order books the deepest, so new traders join CME and rivals like FMX struggle to pull volume away.
With about 3,875 employees producing $6.52 billion of 2025 revenue, its largely fixed cost base gives a 64.9% operating margin that rises as volume grows.

U.S. futures markets support few venues for each benchmark; CME holds dominant positions in U.S. interest rate, equity index, energy, agricultural and metals futures, with ICE the main other large venue.

Incumbent-friendly integrated trading and clearing is its model; newer models such as retail prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket) and 24/7 crypto venues are areas CME is entering rather than counter-positioning against.
Decades of risk management (SPAN and SPAN 2 margining), surveillance and product design are hard to replicate, though technology itself is increasingly outsourced via its Google Cloud partnership.

It holds licences and ownership of key benchmarks (S&P 500 futures licensing through S&P Dow Jones Indices in which it holds a stake, CME Term SOFR) and CFTC-designated contract market status for CME, CBOT, NYMEX and COMEX.

customers.evidence: Clients keep returning in volatile markets: 2025 was a record year for ADV (28.1 million contracts) and revenue ($6.52 billion), and Q3 2026 ADV rose 16.3% with double-digit growth in all six asset classes; no clearing firm exceeded 12% of clearing and transaction fees.

talent.evidence: CME is a well-regarded Chicago financial employer with about 3,875 staff, but it does not appear on major national best-places-to-work lists in recent years.

product.evidence: Its contracts are the global benchmarks for interest rates, U.S. equity indexes, WTI crude, grains and gold, with record non-U.S. activity (about 31% of electronic volume from outside the U.S. in 2025).

ceo.name: Terrence A. (Terry) Duffy
ceo.background: Former CME floor trader who bought a CME membership in 1981; chairman since 2002; attended University of Wisconsin-Whitewater without completing a degree; President and CFO Lynne Fitzpatrick (Brown economics, Chicago Booth MBA) succeeds him as CEO on March 1, 2027

c1.evidence: CME is the world's leading derivatives marketplace with record 2025 ADV of 28.1 million contracts, but futures trading is a mature industry rather than an emerging one, growing about 9% a year in revenue (2022-2025).

c2.evidence: Traders choose CME for the deepest liquidity in benchmark contracts and margin offsets in its clearing house (about $72 billion a day of savings in 2025), an advantage that has lasted decades and is very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: CME is the default leader in futures and the most valuable exchange brand (Brand Finance, 11 years running), but many ordinary people do not know the name.

c4.evidence: CME consistently frames itself as 'where the world comes to manage risk', a meaningful role in global markets, though it has no formal mission statement and management is focused heavily on shareholder returns.

c6.evidence: “Chicago, futures, trading pits” are the first words for most who know it; the impression is mostly positive (essential, reliable, powerful), though some see it as a dominant monopoly-like exchange.

c7.evidence: Demand for hedging grows with government debt, volatility and global participation (record non-U.S. ADV of 9 million in Q3 2026), but derivatives trading is not a fast secular-growth market like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into U.S. Treasury clearing (SEC-approved December 2025), retail prediction markets with FanDuel (launched December 2025), 24/7 crypto trading and cloud-based market access with Google.

m1.evidence: Terry Duffy led the 2007-2008 mergers with CBOT and NYMEX that created today's CME Group and pushed into cloud, retail and Treasury clearing, but he is more a deal-maker and industry advocate than a technology visionary.

m2.evidence: Duffy is not the founder but a lifelong CME member since 1981 who has led it as chairman since 2002, showing long-term commitment; he will step back to executive chairman in March 2027.

m4.evidence: There is little independent evidence on whether Duffy leads in a servant style toward employees and customers.

m5.evidence: CME keeps launching new products (micro contracts grew 32% in 2025, OTC alternatives 11%) but its culture is known more for disciplined execution than for invention.

m6.evidence: Duffy is deeply hands-on with markets as a former floor trader, but he has no engineering background and CME outsources technology infrastructure to Google Cloud.

m7.evidence: Duffy is known for advocacy on market integrity in Congress and co-chairs the Mayo Clinic Greater Chicago Leadership Council, but there is no strong evidence of a mission beyond running a well-functioning, profitable exchange.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Duffy giving a commencement speech at a top university; he received honorary doctorates from DePaul University (2007) and Saint Xavier University (2019).

m8b.evidence: Duffy is a well-known, outspoken figure in finance media and Congress (a former pit trader from Chicago), though not a celebrity CEO on the scale of Elon Musk.

m9.evidence: Under Duffy as CEO since 2017, CME reported a fourth consecutive year of record revenue in 2025 ($6.52 billion) and operating margin rose from 54.0% in 2020 to 64.9% in 2025.

m10.evidence: CME runs lean with about 3,875 employees generating $6.52 billion of revenue (about $1.7 million per employee), though it is not specifically famous for frugality.

c10.evidence: Its markets help farmers, airlines, banks and governments worldwide hedge price risk, indirectly affecting the prices billions pay, but it does not directly touch everyday lives like a consumer product.

p2.evidence: Running a systemically important clearing house that guarantees trillions of dollars of contracts and benchmark price discovery is extremely hard and important to the global financial system.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in four of the last five years: $4.69B (2021, down from $4.88B in 2020), $5.02B, $5.58B, $6.13B and $6.52B (2025).

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose every year from 54.0% (2020) to 56.4%, 60.1%, 61.6%, 64.1% and 64.9% (2025); CME reports no cost of revenue, so gross margin is not meaningful.

f3.evidence: At Sept. 30, 2026 debt was $3.4 billion vs cash of $2.4 billion, small against 2025 net income of $4.07 billion, with positive shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose every year from $2.64 billion (2020) to $4.23 billion (2025); operating cash flow history was not checked for this answer.

v1.evidence: Its benchmark contracts are where the liquidity is, so a trader gets tighter prices and margin offsets on CME that no rival can match for SOFR, Treasury, E-mini S&P 500 or WTI futures.

v2.evidence: CME does not appear on major recent best-places-to-work lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: If CME disappeared overnight, banks, farmers, energy firms and investors worldwide would lose key hedging markets and benchmarks, disrupting interest rates, commodity pricing and financial stability.
